```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(nlme)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(geepack)

load("WtLoss.RData")
```


# part a

```{r}
str(wtloss)

wtloss$diet <- factor(wtloss$diet, levels = c(0, 1, 2))
contrasts(wtloss$diet) <- contr.treatment(
  levels(wtloss$diet),
  base = 1
)

wtloss$id <- factor(wtloss$id)
wtloss <- wtloss[order(wtloss$id, wtloss$time), ]
```


```{r}
# Model (i): random intercept
fit_ri <- lme(
  fixed = weight ~ diet * time,
  random = ~ 1 | id,
  data = wtloss,
  method = "REML"
)


# Model (ii): correlated random intercept and time slope
fit_ris <- lme(
  fixed = weight ~ diet * time,
  random = ~ 1 + time | id,
  data = wtloss,
  method = "REML"
)
```


```{r}
summary(fit_ri)
summary(fit_ris)

VarCorr(fit_ri)
VarCorr(fit_ris)

intervals(fit_ri, which = "fixed")
intervals(fit_ris, which = "fixed")


# Random-effects covariance and correlation matrices
G_ris <- as.matrix(
  getVarCov(fit_ris, type = "random.effects")
)

G_ris
cov2cor(G_ris)

# Residual variance
sigma(fit_ris)^2
```

```{r q1a-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, comment=NA}
terms <- c(
  "(Intercept)", "diet1", "diet2",
  "time", "diet1:time", "diet2:time"
)

labels <- c(
  "Baseline mean: diet 0",
  "Baseline difference: diet 1 vs 0",
  "Baseline difference: diet 2 vs 0",
  "Monthly change: diet 0",
  "Slope difference: diet 1 vs 0",
  "Slope difference: diet 2 vs 0"
)

extract_fixed <- function(fit) {
  tt <- summary(fit)$tTable[terms, , drop = FALSE]
  ci <- intervals(fit, which = "fixed")$fixed[
    terms, , drop = FALSE
  ]

  data.frame(
    estimate = sprintf(
      "%.3f (%.3f, %.3f)",
      tt[, "Value"], ci[, "lower"], ci[, "upper"]
    ),
    p = ifelse(
      tt[, "p-value"] < 0.001,
      "<0.001",
      sprintf("%.3f", tt[, "p-value"])
    )
  )
}

ri <- extract_fixed(fit_ri)
ris <- extract_fixed(fit_ris)

G_ri <- as.matrix(
  getVarCov(fit_ri, type = "random.effects")
)
G_ris <- as.matrix(
  getVarCov(fit_ris, type = "random.effects")
)

fixed_rows <- data.frame(
  Parameter = labels,
  RI = ri$estimate,
  RI_p = ri$p,
  RIS = ris$estimate,
  RIS_p = ris$p
)

random_rows <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c(
    "Random-intercept variance",
    "Random-slope variance",
    "Intercept-slope covariance",
    "Intercept-slope correlation",
    "Residual variance"
  ),
  RI = c(
    sprintf("%.4f", G_ri[1, 1]),
    rep("--", 3),
    sprintf("%.4f", sigma(fit_ri)^2)
  ),
  RI_p = "",
  RIS = sprintf(
    "%.4f",
    c(
      G_ris[1, 1],
      G_ris[2, 2],
      G_ris[1, 2],
      cov2cor(G_ris)[1, 2],
      sigma(fit_ris)^2
    )
  ),
  RIS_p = ""
)

table_data <- rbind(fixed_rows, random_rows)
is_latex <- knitr::is_latex_output()

notes <- paste(
  "Both models were fitted by REML using 997 observations from 120 patients.",
  "Time is in months; month 0 is baseline.",
  "Diet 0 is the reference group: baseline counseling only;",
  "diet 1: counseling at all visits;",
  "diet 2: counseling at all visits plus free exercise-facility access.",
  "Fixed effects are estimates (95% CIs) with model-based t-test p values.",
  "Variance components and the correlation are point estimates only.",
  "A dash indicates a parameter absent from model (i).",
  "Weight is reported in the original, unspecified measurement units."
)

args <- list(
  x = table_data,
  format = if (is_latex) "latex" else "html",
  caption = "Linear mixed-effects models of weight over time.",
  col.names = c(
    "Parameter",
    "Estimate (95% CI)", "p value",
    "Estimate (95% CI)", "p value"
  ),
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
)

if (is_latex) args$booktabs <- TRUE

tab_q1a <- do.call(knitr::kable, args) |>
  add_header_above(
    c(
      " " = 1,
      "Random intercept" = 2,
      "Random intercept and slope" = 2
    )
  ) |>
  pack_rows("Fixed effects", 1, 6) |>
  pack_rows("Variance components", 7, 11)

if (is_latex) {
  tab_q1a <- tab_q1a |>
    column_spec(1, width = "4.2cm") |>
    kable_styling(
      latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"),
      font_size = 9
    )
} else {
  tab_q1a <- tab_q1a |>
    column_spec(1, width = "260px") |>
    kable_styling(
      full_width = FALSE,
      position = "center"
    )
}

tab_q1a <- tab_q1a |>
  footnote(
    general = notes,
    general_title = "Notes: ",
    footnote_as_chunk = TRUE,
    threeparttable = is_latex,
    fixed_small_size = TRUE

tab_q1a
```


\noindent\textbf{Interpretation of model (ii).}

Let $D_{1k}=I(\mathrm{diet}_k=1)$ and
$D_{2k}=I(\mathrm{diet}_k=2)$. The model is
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_{ki} ={}&
\beta_0^*+\beta_1^*D_{1k}+\beta_2^*D_{2k}
+\beta_3^*t_{ki}
+\beta_4^*D_{1k}t_{ki}
+\beta_5^*D_{2k}t_{ki}\\
&+\gamma_{0k}+\gamma_{1k}t_{ki}+\epsilon_{ki},
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\gamma_{0k}\\
\gamma_{1k}
\end{pmatrix}
\sim N\left[
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
G
\right],
\qquad
\epsilon_{ki}\sim N(0,\sigma_\epsilon^2).
\]
Random effects and residual errors are independent, and
patients are independent of one another.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Fixed effects.}

\begin{itemize}
\item $\widehat{\beta}_0^*=250.992$:
The estimated baseline mean weight in diet 0 was
250.992 weight units
(95\% CI: 249.979, 252.004).

\item $\widehat{\beta}_1^*=-0.697$:
At baseline, patients in diet 1 weighed an estimated
0.697 units less than those in diet 0
(95\% CI for the difference: $-2.141$, $0.748$;
$p=0.341$).

\item $\widehat{\beta}_2^*=-2.687$:
At baseline, patients in diet 2 weighed an estimated
2.687 units less than those in diet 0
(95\% CI for the difference: $-4.132$, $-1.243$;
$p<0.001$).

\item $\widehat{\beta}_3^*=0.019$:
Estimated mean weight in diet 0 increased by
0.019 units per month
(95\% CI: $-0.053$, $0.091$; $p=0.607$).
There was insufficient evidence of a nonzero linear
change in this group.

\item $\widehat{\beta}_4^*=-0.102$:
Monthly weight change in diet 1 was
0.102 units lower than in diet 0
(95\% CI for the difference: $-0.201$, $-0.003$;
$p=0.044$).
The estimated slope in diet 1 was
\[
\widehat{\beta}_3^*+\widehat{\beta}_4^*
=-0.083
\]
weight units per month.

\item $\widehat{\beta}_5^*=-0.491$:
Monthly weight change in diet 2 was
0.491 units lower than in diet 0
(95\% CI for the difference: $-0.590$, $-0.393$;
$p<0.001$).
The estimated slope in diet 2 was
\[
\widehat{\beta}_3^*+\widehat{\beta}_5^*
=-0.472
\]
weight units per month.
\end{itemize}

The treatment-specific slopes were calculated before
rounding. They imply estimated average weight losses
of 0.083 and 0.472 units per month in diets 1 and 2,
respectively.

The interaction coefficients represent differences
between slopes. Their $p$ values test these differences
relative to diet 0, rather than testing whether each
treatment group's own slope equals zero.

Because the model uses an identity link and mean-zero
random effects, the fixed-effect trajectories also
describe population mean trajectories within each
treatment group. Individual trajectories vary around
these means through the random intercept and slope.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Variance components.}

The estimated random-effects covariance matrix was
\[
\widehat{G}=
\begin{pmatrix}
10.2416 & -0.2099\\
-0.2099 & 0.0262
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}_\epsilon^2=1.0011.
\]

\begin{itemize}
\item
The random-intercept variance was 10.2416,
corresponding to a standard deviation of
3.200 weight units.
It describes between-patient variation in underlying
baseline weight around the treatment-specific
baseline means.

\item
The random-slope variance was 0.0262,
corresponding to a standard deviation of
0.162 weight units per month.
It describes between-patient variation in underlying
monthly weight change around the treatment-specific
mean slopes.

\item
The intercept--slope covariance was $-0.2099$,
with a correlation of $-0.405$.
Within a treatment group, patients whose underlying
baseline weight was above the group mean tended
to have lower, more negative weight-change slopes,
indicating a greater tendency toward weight loss.

\item
The residual variance was 1.0011,
corresponding to a standard deviation of
1.001 weight units.
It describes variation in observed weights around
each patient's fitted trajectory after accounting
for the fixed and random effects.
\end{itemize}

The intercept and residual variances have units of
squared weight units; the slope variance has units
of squared weight units per month squared; and
the intercept--slope covariance has units of squared
weight units per month. The correlation is dimensionless.



# part b


```{r}
# Use the default simulation algorithm and save the results.
cache_file <- "Q1b_default_REML_seed1504.rds"

if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  sim_b <- readRDS(cache_file)
} else {
  sim_b <- simulate.lme(
    object = fit_ri,
    m2 = fit_ris,
    nsim = 1000,
    seed = 1504,
    method = "REML"
  )

  saveRDS(sim_b, cache_file)
}

null_fit <- sim_b$null$REML
alt_fit <- sim_b$alt$REML

table(
  Null = null_fit[, "info"],
  Alternative = alt_fit[, "info"]
)


# Follow the statistic construction in plot.simulate.lme().
ok <- null_fit[, "info"] == 0 &
      alt_fit[, "info"] == 0 &
      is.finite(null_fit[, "logLik"]) &
      is.finite(alt_fit[, "logLik"])

if (!all(ok)) {
  warning("Only converged simulations are used; inspect the reported count.")
}

T_sim <- 2 * pmax(
  0,
  alt_fit[ok, "logLik"] - null_fit[ok, "logLik"]
)

T_obs <- 2 * as.numeric(
  logLik(fit_ris) - logLik(fit_ri)
)

q95 <- c(
  Simulated = unname(quantile(T_sim, 0.95)),
  Chi_square_1 = qchisq(0.95, df = 1),
  Chi_square_2 = qchisq(0.95, df = 2)
)

critical_values <- data.frame(
  Distribution = names(q95),
  Percentile_95 = unname(q95)
)

test_results <- data.frame(
  Observed_RLRT = T_obs,
  Simulations_used = length(T_sim),
  Bootstrap_p =
    (1 + sum(T_sim >= T_obs)) / (length(T_sim) + 1)
)

critical_values
test_results


# Plot the simulated distribution and theoretical densities.
hist(
  T_sim,
  breaks = 30,
  probability = TRUE,
  col = "grey85",
  border = "white",
  xlim = c(0, max(T_sim, qchisq(0.995, 2))),
  main = "Null distribution of the RLRT statistic",
  xlab = "Restricted likelihood-ratio statistic",
  ylab = "Density"
)

curve(
  dchisq(x, df = 1),
  from = 0.001,
  add = TRUE,
  col = "red3",
  lwd = 2
)

curve(
  dchisq(x, df = 2),
  from = 0,
  add = TRUE,
  col = "blue3",
  lwd = 2
)

abline(
  v = q95,
  col = c("black", "red3", "blue3"),
  lty = 2,
  lwd = 2
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = sprintf(
    c(
      "Simulated: 95%% = %.3f",
      "Chi-square(1): 95%% = %.3f",
      "Chi-square(2): 95%% = %.3f"
    ),
    q95
  ),
  col = c("black", "red3", "blue3"),
  lty = c(2, 1, 1),
  lwd = 2,
  bty = "n",
  cex = 0.85
)
```

Let $\sigma_1^2$ denote the variance of the random time slope
and $\sigma_{01}$ the covariance between the random intercept
and slope. We tested
\[
H_0:\sigma_1^2=0
\quad\text{versus}\quad
H_A:\sigma_1^2>0.
\]
Under $H_0$, positive semidefiniteness of the random-effects
covariance matrix also requires $\sigma_{01}=0$.
Under $H_A$, this covariance is estimated without being
restricted to zero.

This is a nonstandard testing problem because a variance
of zero lies on the boundary of the parameter space.
For this model comparison, the asymptotic reference
distribution is
\[
\frac{1}{2}\chi_1^2+\frac{1}{2}\chi_2^2,
\]
rather than a conventional chi-square distribution based
solely on the number of additional parameters.

We used \texttt{simulate.lme()} to generate 1,000 datasets
under the fitted random-intercept model, with seed 1504.
Both models were fitted by REML to each simulated dataset.
The observed restricted likelihood-ratio statistic was
\[
T_{\mathrm{obs}}
=
2\left\{
\ell_R(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{RIS}})
-
\ell_R(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{RI}})
\right\}
=
72.899.
\]

The simulated null distribution was right-skewed.
Its estimated 95th percentile was 4.529, between the
corresponding percentiles of the $\chi_1^2$ and $\chi_2^2$
distributions, 3.841 and 5.991, respectively.
Relative to the simulated critical value, using
$\chi_1^2$ alone would give a lower rejection threshold,
whereas using $\chi_2^2$ alone would give a higher threshold.

The observed statistic was substantially greater than
the simulated 95th percentile. None of the 1,000 simulated
statistics was as large as the observed statistic.
Using the Monte Carlo correction, the estimated
bootstrap $p$ value was
\[
\widehat{p}
=
\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^{1000}
I(T_b\geq T_{\mathrm{obs}})}
{1000+1}
=
\frac{1}{1001}
\approx 0.001.
\]

We therefore reject $H_0$ at the 5\% significance level.
The random-intercept and random-slope model provides
a significantly better fit than the random-intercept-only
model. After accounting for treatment group and its
interaction with time, patients still differ in their
rates of weight change. The random-intercept-only model
is therefore inadequate to describe this between-patient
variation in longitudinal trajectories.


# part c


```{r}
# Conditional standardized residuals
diag_data <- getData(fit_ri)

diag_data$fitted <- as.numeric(
  fitted(fit_ri, level = 1)
)

diag_data$residual <- as.numeric(
  residuals(fit_ri, level = 1, type = "pearson")
)

vg <- Variogram(
  fit_ri,
  form = ~ time | id,
  resType = "pearson"
)

old_par <- par(
  mfrow = c(2, 2),
  mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1)
)


# Residuals versus fitted values
plot(
  diag_data$fitted,
  diag_data$residual,
  pch = 16,
  col = adjustcolor("black", alpha.f = 0.3),
  xlab = "Conditional fitted weight",
  ylab = "Standardized residual",
  main = "Residuals vs fitted values"
)

abline(h = 0, col = "grey50", lty = 2)

lines(
  lowess(diag_data$fitted, diag_data$residual),
  col = "red3",
  lwd = 2
)


# Residual distribution over time
boxplot(
  residual ~ time,
  data = diag_data,
  col = "grey90",
  xlab = "Month",
  ylab = "Standardized residual",
  main = "Residuals by month"
)

abline(h = 0, col = "red3", lty = 2)


# Residual normality
qqnorm(
  diag_data$residual,
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.5,
  main = "Normal Q-Q plot of residuals"
)

qqline(
  diag_data$residual,
  col = "red3",
  lwd = 2
)


# Within-patient residual dependence
plot(
  vg$dist,
  vg$variog,
  type = "b",
  pch = 16,
  xlab = "Time lag (months)",
  ylab = "Semivariance",
  main = "Residual semivariogram"
)

abline(h = 1, col = "red3", lty = 2)

par(old_par)

vg[, c("dist", "variog", "n.pairs")]
```



The standardized conditional residuals were generally centered
near zero, and the residual-versus-fitted plot showed no strong
systematic trend or pronounced funnel shape. The monthly
boxplots showed some differences in residual location and
spread. The normal Q--Q plot was approximately linear,
with modest departures in the tails and a few extreme
residuals, suggesting that normality was broadly reasonable.

The residual semivariogram, however, showed a clear increase
with time lag. The estimated semivariance increased from
0.784 at a one-month lag to 2.328 at a ten-month lag.
Under the random-intercept model with independent,
homoscedastic residual errors, the standardized residual
semivariogram would be expected to be approximately flat
near 1. The observed pattern therefore suggests that the
model does not adequately capture the within-patient
covariance structure. Estimates at the longest lags are
less precise because they are based on relatively few pairs,
particularly 41 pairs at ten months and 15 pairs at eleven months.

These findings are consistent with part (b), where the
random-intercept-only model was rejected in favor of the
random-intercept and random-slope model
($T_{\mathrm{obs}}=72.899$, bootstrap $p\approx0.001$).
The increasing semivariance is consistent with unmodeled
between-patient variation in rates of weight change,
supporting the inclusion of random time slopes.


# part d


```{r}
gee_data <- wtloss[order(wtloss$id, wtloss$time), ]

gee_data$id <- factor(gee_data$id)
gee_data$diet <- factor(
  gee_data$diet,
  levels = c(0, 1, 2)
)

contrasts(gee_data$diet) <- contr.treatment(
  levels(gee_data$diet),
  base = 1
)

gee_data$visit <- gee_data$time + 1L


# Working independence
fit_gee_i <- geeglm(
  weight ~ diet * time,
  id = id,
  waves = visit,
  data = gee_data,
  family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
  corstr = "independence",
  scale.fix = FALSE,
  std.err = "san.se"
)


# Working exchangeable
fit_gee_e <- geeglm(
  weight ~ diet * time,
  id = id,
  waves = visit,
  data = gee_data,
  family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
  corstr = "exchangeable",
  scale.fix = FALSE,
  std.err = "san.se"
)


# Working AR(1)
fit_gee_ar1 <- geeglm(
  weight ~ diet * time,
  id = id,
  waves = visit,
  data = gee_data,
  family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
  corstr = "ar1",
  scale.fix = FALSE,
  std.err = "san.se"
)

summary(fit_gee_i)
summary(fit_gee_e)
summary(fit_gee_ar1)
```


```{r q1d-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, comment=NA}
coef_order <- c(
  "(Intercept)", "diet1", "diet2",
  "time", "diet1:time", "diet2:time"
)

labels <- c(
  "Baseline mean: diet 0",
  "Baseline difference: diet 1 vs 0",
  "Baseline difference: diet 2 vs 0",
  "Monthly change: diet 0",
  "Slope difference: diet 1 vs 0",
  "Slope difference: diet 2 vs 0"
)

extract_gee <- function(fit) {
  tt <- summary(fit)$coefficients[
    coef_order, , drop = FALSE
  ]

  estimate <- tt[, "Estimate"]
  se <- tt[, "Std.err"]

  sprintf(
    "%.4f (%.4f, %.4f)",
    estimate,
    estimate - qnorm(0.975) * se,
    estimate + qnorm(0.975) * se
  )
}

fixed_rows <- data.frame(
  Parameter = labels,
  I = extract_gee(fit_gee_i),
  E = extract_gee(fit_gee_e),
  AR1 = extract_gee(fit_gee_ar1)
)

working_rows <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c(
    "Working correlation parameter",
    "Dispersion parameter"
  ),
  I = sprintf(
    "%.4f",
    c(0, fit_gee_i$geese$gamma[1])
  ),
  E = sprintf(
    "%.4f",
    c(
      fit_gee_e$geese$alpha[1],
      fit_gee_e$geese$gamma[1]
    )
  ),
  AR1 = sprintf(
    "%.4f",
    c(
      fit_gee_ar1$geese$alpha[1],
      fit_gee_ar1$geese$gamma[1]
    )
  )
)

table_data <- rbind(fixed_rows, working_rows)
is_latex <- knitr::is_latex_output()

args <- list(
  x = table_data,
  format = if (is_latex) "latex" else "html",
  caption = paste(
    "GEE estimates of weight trajectories",
    "under three working correlation structures."
  ),
  col.names = c("Parameter", "GEE-I", "GEE-E", "GEE-AR1"),
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
)

if (is_latex) args$booktabs <- TRUE

tab_q1d <- do.call(knitr::kable, args) |>
  pack_rows("Regression parameters", 1, 6) |>
  pack_rows("Working covariance parameters", 7, 8)

if (is_latex) {
  tab_q1d <- tab_q1d |>
    column_spec(1, width = "3.8cm") |>
    kable_styling(
      latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"),
      font_size = 9
    )
} else {
  tab_q1d <- tab_q1d |>
    column_spec(1, width = "250px") |>
    kable_styling(
      full_width = FALSE,
      position = "center"
    )
}

notes <- paste(
  "GEE-I, working independence; GEE-E, working exchangeable;",
  "GEE-AR1, working first-order autoregressive correlation.",
  "All models used an identity link and the same mean model,",
  "with 997 observations from 120 patients.",
  "Regression entries are estimates (95% robust sandwich Wald CIs).",
  "Working covariance parameters are point estimates only.",
  "Diet 0 is the reference: baseline counseling only;",
  "diet 1: counseling at all visits;",
  "diet 2: counseling at all visits plus free exercise-facility access.",
  "Time is in months, with month 0 representing baseline.",
  "For GEE-AR1, the correlation parameter refers to a one-month lag;",
  "for GEE-I it is fixed at zero.",
  "Weight is reported in the original, unspecified measurement units."
)

tab_q1d <- tab_q1d |>
  footnote(
    general = notes,
    general_title = "Notes: ",
    footnote_as_chunk = TRUE,
    threeparttable = is_latex,
    fixed_small_size = TRUE
  )

tab_q1d
```


For the GEE-E analysis, the marginal mean model was
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(Y_{ki}\mid D_{1k},D_{2k},t_{ki})
={}&\beta_0+\beta_1D_{1k}+\beta_2D_{2k}
+\beta_3t_{ki}\\
&+\beta_4D_{1k}t_{ki}
+\beta_5D_{2k}t_{ki},
\end{aligned}
\]
where $D_{1k}=I(\mathrm{diet}_k=1)$ and
$D_{2k}=I(\mathrm{diet}_k=2)$.
Diet 0 was the reference group, and $t=0$ represented
baseline. Confidence intervals and $p$ values were based
on robust sandwich standard errors.

\begin{itemize}
\item $\widehat{\beta}_0=250.9455$:
The estimated population mean baseline weight in diet 0
was 250.9455 weight units
(95\% CI: 249.8502, 252.0407).

\item $\widehat{\beta}_1=-0.6464$:
At baseline, the population mean weight in diet 1 was
an estimated 0.6464 units lower than in diet 0
(95\% CI for the difference: $-2.0892$, $0.7965$;
$p=0.380$).
There was insufficient evidence of a baseline
mean difference between these groups.

\item $\widehat{\beta}_2=-2.6607$:
At baseline, the population mean weight in diet 2 was
an estimated 2.6607 units lower than in diet 0
(95\% CI for the difference: $-4.1276$, $-1.1938$;
$p<0.001$).

\item $\widehat{\beta}_3=0.0398$:
In diet 0, population mean weight increased by an
estimated 0.0398 units per month
(95\% CI: $-0.0285$, $0.1081$; $p=0.253$).
There was insufficient evidence of a nonzero
linear change in this group.

\item $\widehat{\beta}_4=-0.1235$:
The monthly change in population mean weight in diet 1
was 0.1235 units lower than in diet 0
(95\% CI for the difference: $-0.2311$, $-0.0160$;
$p=0.024$).
The estimated slope in diet 1 was
\[
\widehat{\beta}_3+\widehat{\beta}_4
\approx -0.084
\]
weight units per month.

\item $\widehat{\beta}_5=-0.5002$:
The monthly change in population mean weight in diet 2
was 0.5002 units lower than in diet 0
(95\% CI for the difference: $-0.5986$, $-0.4018$;
$p<0.001$).
The estimated slope in diet 2 was
\[
\widehat{\beta}_3+\widehat{\beta}_5
\approx -0.460
\]
weight units per month.
\end{itemize}

Thus, the estimated population mean trajectories
corresponded to average monthly weight losses of
approximately 0.084 and 0.460 units in diets 1 and 2,
respectively. The interaction coefficients represent
differences between treatment-specific slopes;
their $p$ values do not test whether each group's
own slope equals zero.

The estimated exchangeable working correlation was
0.8583, indicating strong within-patient association
under a working model that assigns the same correlation
to every pair of measurements from the same patient.


# part e


```{r}
# Joint robust Wald test of the diet-by-time interactions.
interaction_terms <- c("diet1:time", "diet2:time")

b <- coef(fit_gee_e)[interaction_terms]

V <- vcov(fit_gee_e)[
  interaction_terms,
  interaction_terms,
  drop = FALSE
]

wald_stat <- as.numeric(
  t(b) %*% solve(V, b)
)

df <- length(b)

p_value <- pchisq(
  wald_stat,
  df = df,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

wald_results <- data.frame(
  Wald_statistic = wald_stat,
  df = df,
  p_value = p_value
)

wald_results


# Estimated population mean weight change per month.
beta <- coef(fit_gee_e)

slope_results <- data.frame(
  Diet = c("0", "1", "2"),
  Monthly_weight_change = c(
    beta["time"],
    beta["time"] + beta["diet1:time"],
    beta["time"] + beta["diet2:time"]
  ),
  row.names = NULL
)

slope_results
```


We tested whether the population mean rates of weight
change were equal across the three treatment groups:
\[
H_0:\beta_4=\beta_5=0
\quad\text{versus}\quad
H_A:\text{at least one of }\beta_4,\beta_5
\text{ is nonzero}.
\]

Using the GEE-E estimates and their robust sandwich
covariance matrix, the joint Wald test gave
\[
W\approx105,\qquad df=2,\qquad
p=1.71\times10^{-23}.
\]
We therefore reject $H_0$ and conclude that the average
rate of weight change differs among the treatment groups.

For a non-biostatistician collaborator, these results
can be summarized as follows:

There is strong evidence that the treatment groups
had different average weight-change rates.
Patients receiving counseling only at baseline had
an estimated average weight increase of 0.0398 units
per month. Patients receiving counseling at every visit
had an estimated average weight loss of 0.0837 units
per month, while those also offered free access to an
exercise facility had an estimated average weight loss
of 0.4604 units per month. The largest estimated average
weight loss was therefore observed in the counseling-plus-exercise
group. These are population averages; individual patients
may have different weight-change patterns.
